name: Tumbuka
sweep_summary: Tumbuka (tumb1250) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Downing 2006 (ZASPiL 43), was fetched sources open access and read: it is first-hand fieldwork and states that Chitumbuka has no lexical tone contrasts and that every word in isolation lengthens its penult and bears a falling H tone, with the H 'aligned with the stressed penult' (pp. 57-58); fn. 1 records that Kisseberth & Odden 2003 classify the language as a stress language while Downing calls the system more tone-like (predictable pitch accent). Two further first-hand Downing papers were obtained and read (2008 ZASPiL 49, already on file from the Zulu fetch; 2012 ACAL 42 from lingref) and restate fixed penult lengthening as the correlate of phrasal and sentence stress, not moved by focus. Chavula 2016 (LOT 423, native speaker) says Citumbuka is not tonal and notes penultimate stress as a cue in intensive vs causative suffixes but gives no placement rule. Elmslie 1891 (archive.org) is silent. Unread: Downing 2010 'Accent in African languages' (De Gruyter, paywalled; medium priority), Kisseberth & Odden 2003 (print), Kiso 2012 (DiVA unreachable), Young 1932 (no open copy; Recommended coding for a new catalog record: fixed penultimate prominence (length + falling tone), no lexical tone; classification as stress vs predictable pitch-accent is contested in the source itself. All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: there are no lexical or grammatical tonal contrasts in Chitumbuka. The penult of every word in isolation is lengthened and bears a falling tone [...] In sum, the word-level tone system of Chitumbuka has many defining properties of a pitch-accent language (Downing 2003, to appear; Hyman 1977; Odden 1999): obligatoriness and culminativity: every word has one and only one High tone; positional restrictions: only the penult can bear a High tone; and tone-stress interaction: the High tone aligns with the stressed penult.
new_statements.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2006. The prosody and syntax of focus in Chitumbuka. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 43: 55-79. doi:10.21248/zaspil.43.2006.285
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.1 'Words in isolation', pp. 57-58 (with fn. 1, p. 58)
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word prominence: every word in isolation has a lengthened penult carrying a falling (H) tone, with no lexical tone contrasts; phrase-medially the lengthening is lost. Kisseberth & Odden 2003 call this a stress language (fixed penult); Downing prefers to call it a predictable pitch-accent system that is 'more tone-like than stress-like'. Either way the placement is fixed on the penult, with culminative extra lengthening on the sentence-final penult. First-hand fieldwork data.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2006. The prosody and syntax of focus in Chitumbuka. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 43 (Papers in Bantu grammar and description): 55-79. doi:10.21248/zaspil.43.2006.285
sources.quote: there are no lexical or grammatical tonal contrasts in Chitumbuka. The penult of every word in isolation is lengthened and bears a falling tone [...] In sum, the word-level tone system of Chitumbuka has many defining properties of a pitch-accent language (Downing 2003, to appear; Hyman 1977; Odden 1999): obligatoriness and culminativity: every word has one and only one High tone; positional restrictions: only the penult can bear a High tone; and tone-stress interaction: the High tone aligns with the stressed penult.
sources.locator: sec. 2.1 'Words in isolation', pp. 57-58, and fn. 1 p. 58; sec. 2.2 p. 59
sources.note: First-hand fieldwork (consultant Dymon Kondowe). Word-level prominence is fixed on the penult of every word in isolation: the penult vowel is lengthened and carries a falling (H) tone; no lexical or grammatical tone contrasts. Phrase-medial words lose the lengthening (sec. 2.2). Fn. 1: 'For these reasons Kisseberth & Odden (2003) classify Chitumbuka as a stress language. However... This makes Chitumbuka's pitch system more tone-like than stress-like.' At the utterance level there is extra penult lengthening on the last phrase (sentence 'stress', p. 59). So: fixed penultimate prominence realis…

sources.citation: Chavula, Jean Josephine. 2016. Verbal derivation and valency in Citumbuka. LOT Dissertation Series 423. Utrecht: LOT (PhD, Leiden University).
sources.quote: Citumbuka is not a tonal language. It has five vowels and all of them are short in quality [...] (p. 11) — There are two major differences between the intensive and causative in Citumbuka. Firstly, the intensive does not introduce a new argument; and secondly, the penultimate syllable is more stressed in an intensive than a causative. In this thesis, the intensive suffix is therefore, presented as -ísk/ésk- (p. 155)
sources.note: Native-speaker morphosyntax thesis; no phonology sketch of stress placement (the author recommends a phonology study, p. 226). States that Citumbuka is not tonal and notes penultimate stress as the cue distinguishing intensive -ísk- from causative -isk-, which presupposes penultimate prominence but gives no general placement rule.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2012. On the (non-)congruence of focus and prominence in Tumbuka. In Michael R. Marlo et al. (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 42nd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 122-133. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
sources.quote: it is controversial whether Tumbuka is to be considered a tone language because, except for with some ideophones (Vail 1972), there are no lexical or grammatical tonal contrasts. Rather, the penult of every word in isolation is lengthened and bears a falling tone [...] Because the (phrase) penult predictably has a High tone and lengthened vowel, Tumbuka is often classified as a stress language (Kisseberth & Odden 2003). [...] penult lengthening is considered the principal correlate of phrasal and sentential stress prominence in Tumbuka.
sources.locator: sec. 2 'Sketch of Tumbuka prosody', pp. 122-124; sec. 3.1 p. 126
sources.note: Restates Downing 2006/2008 with the same data: fixed penult lengthening + falling tone on every word in isolation, reduced phrase-medially; culminative sentence stress on the final word's penult; adds the note that the system plausibly arose from penult lengthening plus H-attraction to the penult with loss of tonal contrasts (p. 123).

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2008. Focus and prominence in Chichewa, Chitumbuka and Durban Zulu. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 49: 47-65. doi:10.21248/zaspil.49.2008.363
sources.quote: In all three languages, lengthening of the phrase penult syllable is the easiest to identify – and most consistent – correlate of prosodic phrasing. [...] In all three of these Bantu languages, though, the highest degree of stress (defined as vowel lengthening) in the sentence is fixed on the penult syllable of the final prosodic phrase in the sentence. [...] phrase stress falls consistently on the phrase penult syllable.
sources.note: First-hand (Downing fieldwork). Stress = penult vowel lengthening, fixed on the penult of each phonological phrase and culminative on the sentence-final phrase; not attracted by focus. Phrase-level statement consistent with the word-level penult statement of Downing 2006.
